questions.prompt: A firewall policy has an application rule allowing only *.contoso.com, and a network rule allowing TCP 443 to any destination in a lower-priority rule collection group. A VM reaches an arbitrary external site over HTTPS. Why?
options: Application rules apply only to HTTP, so HTTPS bypasses them
The network rule matched first, and a network rule match stops processing before application rules run
The lower-priority group is evaluated first, overriding the application rule
Threat intelligence allowed the traffic because the destination is not known-malicious
questions.explanation: Azure Firewall processes DNAT, then network, then application rules - always in that order, regardless of rule collection group priority or policy inheritance. A network rule match ends processing, so a broad network allow silently disables FQDN filtering even when the application rule is perfectly correct.
why_not: Application rules handle HTTPS as well as HTTP. The problem is that they were never reached.
Rule collection group priority does not change the rule-type order. Network rules are processed before application rules, whatever the group priority.
Threat intelligence did not allow anything. The network rule matched and ended processing.

questions.sub_skill: Configure Azure private endpoints to secure access to Azure platform as a service (PaaS) resources
questions.prompt: You create a private endpoint for a storage account and confirm a VM in the virtual network resolves it to a private address. A colleague at home still reaches the same account over the internet. What is required so that only the virtual network can reach it?
options: Nothing further; DNS propagation will complete within 24 hours
Set the storage account's public network access to disabled, or its firewall to deny
Add the colleague's address to the private DNS zone as an exclusion
Convert the private endpoint to a service endpoint
questions.explanation: Creating a private endpoint does not close the public door. The service's public endpoint stays reachable until you separately set that service's network rules. A private endpoint alongside an open public endpoint is a more expensive version of no change.
why_not: DNS is already working: the VM resolves the private address. The public endpoint stays open until you close it.
A private DNS zone has no per-client exclusions. It answers queries from linked virtual networks, and the colleague at home never queries it.
A service endpoint does not remove the public endpoint either. The fix is the account's own network settings.

questions.sub_skill: Configure Azure private endpoints to secure access to Azure platform as a service (PaaS) resources
questions.prompt: A private endpoint works from the virtual network but not from an on-premises host over ExpressRoute, and nslookup from on-premises returns a public address. What is missing?
options: The private endpoint must be recreated in the on-premises region
Hybrid DNS resolution - the private DNS zone must be reachable from on-premises
A service endpoint on the gateway subnet
The storage firewall must allow the on-premises public egress address
questions.explanation: Resolving the name from outside the virtual network returns the public endpoint by design. DNS is the whole implementation of a private endpoint, and making it work for on-premises clients is a separate piece of hybrid DNS forwarding work.
why_not: Private endpoints are reachable from on-premises over ExpressRoute. The endpoint is fine; name resolution is not.
Service endpoints do not apply to traffic from on-premises, and the failure here is DNS returning the public address.
Allowing the public address would make the connection work over the internet, which bypasses the private endpoint rather than fixing it.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure Microsoft Entra Private Access
questions.prompt: A legacy internal application on TCP 8443 must be reachable by remote staff with MFA and device compliance enforced, without a VPN. Which component makes the Conditional Access requirement possible?
options: The Global Secure Access client, which evaluates policy on the device
The private network connector, which authenticates users before forwarding
Publication as an enterprise application, so Conditional Access policies can be assigned to it
The Private Access traffic forwarding profile, which carries the policy
questions.explanation: Both Quick Access and per-app access publish the resource as an enterprise application. Because it is an enterprise app, users and groups are assigned to it and Conditional Access governs it - which is precisely what a VPN gateway cannot do, since it authenticates once at the tunnel and then routes.
why_not: The client captures traffic and forwards it to Global Secure Access. What Conditional Access policy is assigned to is the enterprise application.
The connector brokers traffic into the private network. It is not where users are authenticated or where policy is assigned.
The forwarding profile controls which traffic the client sends through Global Secure Access. Policy on this application comes from publishing it as an enterprise application.

questions.sub_skill: Evaluate effective security rules by using Azure Network Watcher diagnostics
questions.prompt: Traffic from a spoke VM is not reaching the firewall, although the firewall rules are correct. Which Network Watcher tool would you use first, and what result confirms the problem?
options: IP flow verify - a Deny result naming the firewall policy
Next hop - a result of Internet rather than VirtualAppliance
Effective security rules - a missing application rule
Connection troubleshoot - a failure at the DNS stage
questions.explanation: Next hop answers where a packet actually goes. If it returns Internet instead of VirtualAppliance with the firewall's private address, the route table is not associated with the subnet and every firewall rule is decorative. IP flow verify evaluates NSGs and admin rules, not firewall policy - knowing which tool answers which question is the skill being tested.
why_not: IP flow verify evaluates NSGs and security admin rules, not firewall policy, so it cannot name one.
Effective security rules shows the NSG rules applied to a NIC. It knows nothing about firewall application rules - and the firewall rules are correct anyway.
The symptom is traffic not reaching the firewall, which is a routing question. Next hop answers it directly.

questions.sub_skill: Configure Azure Private Link services to secure access to network resources
questions.prompt: An internal API runs on VMs behind a Standard Load Balancer in your virtual network. A partner in another Microsoft Entra tenant must reach it privately. Their address space overlaps yours, you will not peer the networks or expose a public IP, and you must decide which partner connections are allowed. What should you configure?
options: A private endpoint for the load balancer in your own virtual network, shared with the partner
A Private Link service on the Standard Load Balancer; the partner creates a private endpoint to its alias, and you approve the connection request
Virtual network peering across the two tenants, restricted by NSG rules to the partner's address range
A service endpoint on the API subnet, with the partner's subnet added to the allow list
questions.explanation: Private Link service publishes your own service behind a Standard Load Balancer. The consumer references its alias from a private endpoint in their own network, the connection arrives as a request you approve or reject, and NAT on the provider side means overlapping address space does not matter.
why_not: A private endpoint is the consumer side: it gives a network a private IP for someone else's service. The partner needs the endpoint in their network, pointing at a service you publish.
Peering is ruled out by the requirement, and virtual networks with overlapping address spaces cannot be peered in any case.
Service endpoints extend a subnet's identity to Azure platform services such as Storage or SQL Database. They cannot publish your own application to another tenant's network.
questions.concept: Private Link service (provider side) versus private endpoint (consumer side)
questions.misconception: The provider creates the private endpoint
